doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Riverside and the New York scene
title: Buddy Rich and the drum solo at Westbury
summary: Working with Buddy Rich on Long Island, Ware slides behind the drums for eight bars and never works with Rich again.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: and John Bunce; in fact, Buddy and I did call me up to do a commercial for Alcoa Aluminum, just bass and drums, and I don't know whether that was the end results, but I got paid for it, and then we had -- we got the Cork and Bob out in (unintelligible) at Westbury, Long Island, and I had worked out there before; I worked with my own little trio, and had worked with some other people, and tried to ... a fellow named Charlie Graziano who owned the place -- jazz buff.

And this particular night, the place was just jammed because you know, I told you, I played drums occasionally, and we were playing and I'm standing right behind Buddy, and when we finished, [unintelligible] I took the subway over and Buddy got up from his set and was bounding toward me with his sticks in his hand, you know, and somebody in the crowd hollered, "Play some drums, Wilbur" and I thought Buddy was offering me the sticks, so I got the sticks out of his hand, and slid in the seat and looked over to the other and said, "I'm taking 8 bars" and I went in to the eight bar solo and I was gonna play some drums. I wasn't thinking that I was gonna sit down and try to show Buddy up or cut him or nothing; I'm just going along entertaining, and I thought that was what Buddy meant for me to do.
And I played ... I went on as a solo, and that night was the end of that. I never worked with Buddy Rich no more. It was in bad taste, probably, but I wasn't looking at it like
that; I was just having fun, you know. Oh, I had beautiful jobs, beautiful gigs.
